questions.question_text: What is the leading term of $P(x) = 4x^{4} - 3x^{3} + 8$?

options.why: Selected the term with power $3$ instead of the highest power $4$.
Selected the constant term instead of the highest-degree term.
Gave the leading coefficient instead of the leading term.

questions.solution_text:
The highest power is $4$.
The leading term is $4x^{4}$.

questions.question_text: What is the leading term of $P(x) = 3 - 2x + 6x^{2} - 7x^{3}$?

options.why: Dropped the negative sign from the highest-degree term.
Selected the highest positive term instead of the highest-degree term.
Selected the first written term instead of the highest-degree term.

questions.solution_text:
The highest power is $3$.
The leading term is $-7x^{3}$.

questions.question_text: What is the leading term of $P(x) = -2(x - 3)(2x + 1)(x + 4)$?

options.why: Omitted the coefficient $2$ from the factor $(2x + 1)$.
Dropped the negative sign on the front coefficient $-2$.
Counted only two of the three linear factors when adding the powers.

questions.question_text: What is the leading term of $P(x) = (4 - x)^{2}(x + 2)(3 - x)$?

options.why: Treated $(-x)^{2}$ as $-x^{2}$, giving the wrong product sign.
Kept the negative coefficient but incorrectly added the powers $2+1+1$ to get $3$ instead of $4$.
Multiplied the constant terms $4^{2}\times 2\times 3$ instead of the highest-power terms.

options.text: Even degree because both ends point downwards, with a negative leading coefficient
Even degree because both ends point downwards, with a positive leading coefficient
options.why: Identified even degree but mistakenly thought pointing towards $-\infty$ means positive.

options.text: Odd degree because the curve has turning points, with a negative leading coefficient
options.why: Confused turning points with an odd degree when both ends clearly point in the same direction.

options.text: Odd degree because both ends point downwards, with a positive leading coefficient
options.why: Incorrectly claimed that ends pointing in the same direction implies odd degree.

questions.solution_text:
Both ends point in the same direction (downwards), so the degree is **even**.
Because the ends point towards $-\infty$, the leading coefficient is **negative**.

options.text: Odd degree and positive leading coefficient
Odd degree and negative leading coefficient
options.why: Read the left end pointing down as indicating a negative coefficient; the right end determines the sign.

options.text: Even degree and positive leading coefficient
options.why: Treated ends pointing in opposite directions as indicating even degree.

options.text: Even degree and negative leading coefficient
options.why: Treated opposite end directions as even degree and reversed the coefficient sign despite the right end pointing up.

questions.solution_text:
The ends point in opposite directions, so the degree is **odd**.
The right end points up, so the leading coefficient is **positive**.

questions.question_text: What is the leading term of $P(x) = (2x - 3)(x + 4)(x - 5)$?

options.why: Used the negative constant in a factor to assign the sign of the leading term.
Omitted the coefficient $2$ from $(2x - 3)$.
Counted only two linear factors when adding the powers.

questions.question_text: What is the leading term of $P(x) = (5 - 2x)^{3}(3x + 1)^{2}$?

options.why: Treated the odd power $(-2x)^{3}$ as positive.
Multiplied $-2$ and $3$ without raising these coefficients to powers $3$ and $2$.
Multiplied the factor degrees $3$ and $2$ instead of adding them.
